CAS Monograph 15, *Introduction to Capital Modeling and Portfolio Management*
(John Major and Stephen Mildenhall, 2026), shows how an insurer can price its
risk and split the price over its business units, from a distribution of
outcomes alone. Its worked examples run in Mildenhall's Python package
`aggregate`. This guide runs them in prospicio from R and prints both sets of
numbers next to each other, so you can see what the method does, what each
step costs in code, and where the two programs agree or differ.

This is the R twin of the Python guide
[`capital-modeling-monograph-15.md`](capital-modeling-monograph-15.md): the
same sections, the same examples and the same numbers. The R package calls the
same Rust code as the Python one, so the parameters, premiums and allocations
agree to every digit printed, including the Iman-Conover samples drawn by seed.

The text of the monograph is the authors'; what follows is an explanation in
new words with the numbers recomputed. Read the monograph for the reasoning
(its chapters 3 to 6 and 8) and this guide for the mechanics (its chapter 9).
Table numbers below are the monograph's. Money is in the units of its
examples.

Each R chunk is followed by the text it prints.
`R/prospicio/tests/test-guides.R` runs the chunks in order and requires each
one to print exactly that text, so a number below cannot go stale when the
library changes. To render the page, install the R package
(`remotes::install_github`, see `R/prospicio/bootstrap.R`) and run
`quarto render docs/guides/capital-modeling-monograph-15.qmd`.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(prospicio)

# Thousands separators, as Python's {:,.0f}. Rounding first rounds a half to
# even, as Python does, on every platform's C library.
comma <- function(x, digits = 0) {
  formatC(round(x, digits), format = "f", digits = digits, big.mark = ",")
}
```

## 1. The example company

The monograph's running example, InsCo, has three units, A, B and C, and ten
equally likely simulated years. Each row is a year and each cell the unit's
loss in it:

```{r}
ROWS <- rbind(
  c(5, 20, 11), c(7, 33, 0), c(15, 13, 0), c(15, 7, 0), c(13, 20, 7),
  c(5, 27, 8), c(15, 16, 9), c(26, 19, 10), c(17, 8, 40), c(16, 20, 64)
)
colnames(ROWS) <- c("A", "B", "C")
insco <- capital_portfolio(ROWS)
totals <- rowSums(ROWS)

for (name in c("A", "B", "C", "Total")) {
  losses <- if (name == "Total") totals else ROWS[, name]
  s <- sampled(losses)
  sd <- sqrt(variance(s)) # sampled() divides by n, as the monograph does
  cat(sprintf("%-6s mean %6.2f  cv %.3f\n", name, mean(s), sd / mean(s)))
}
```

```text
A      mean  13.40  cv 0.453
B      mean  18.30  cv 0.412
C      mean  14.90  cv 1.324
Total  mean  46.60  cv 0.455
```

This is Table 9.1's last two rows: means of 13.4, 18.3, 14.9 and 46.6, and CVs
of 0.453, 0.412, 1.324 and 0.455. Unit C is the volatile one: a small mean, and
a 64 in the worst year. A `capital_portfolio()` is built from the matrix of
rows directly, one named column per unit, so there is no frequency-severity
model or grid here, and no approximation: every number below is computed on the
ten years as they are.

Pricing works on the distinct totals, not on the years. Four of the years (the
second, fifth, sixth and seventh) all total 40, so the portfolio keeps one
scenario at 40 with probability 0.4 and each unit's average loss given that
total, which the monograph calls its conditional expectation, `kappa`.
`portfolio_kappa(port, unit)` returns a unit's, one value per distinct total
(Python's `Portfolio.kappa(unit)`):

```{r}
cat("totals ", insco@totals, "\n")
cat("probs  ", round(insco@probs, 1), "\n")
for (unit in c("A", "B", "C")) {
  k <- portfolio_kappa(insco, unit) # E[X_unit | X = total]
  cat(sprintf("kappa %s", unit), sprintf("%.2f", k), "\n")
}
```

```text
totals  22 28 36 40 55 65 100
probs   0.1 0.1 0.1 0.4 0.1 0.1 0.1
kappa A 15.00 15.00 5.00 10.00 26.00 17.00 16.00
kappa B 7.00 13.00 20.00 24.00 19.00 8.00 20.00
kappa C 0.00 0.00 11.00 6.00 10.00 40.00 64.00
```

At a total of 40, A is expected to lose 10, B 24 and C 6, the row of Table 9.4.
The conditional expectations always add up to the total, so splitting the
portfolio's price by them can never create or lose money.

## 2. The capital standard

A price needs a capital standard: how many assets stand behind the book. The
monograph's chapter 3 introduces value at risk (VaR, a quantile) and tail value
at risk (TVaR, the average above it). The `aggregate` package, and prospicio,
read a standard of "p" as assets equal to the p quantile of the total:
`portfolio_assets(port, p)` (Python's `Portfolio.assets(p)`), the level
`natural_price(port, d, p = p)` prices at, whatever the distortion `d`:

```{r}
total <- sampled(totals)
cat(sprintf("%5s %6s %8s  assets at p\n", "p", "VaR", "TVaR"))
for (p in c(0.8, 0.85, 0.9, 1.0)) {
  cat(sprintf("%5.2f %6.0f %8.3f  %.0f\n", p, quantile(total, p), TVaR(total, p),
              portfolio_assets(insco, p)))
}
```

```text
    p    VaR     TVaR  assets at p
 0.80     55   82.500  55
 0.85     65   88.333  65
 0.90     65  100.000  65
 1.00    100  100.000  100
```

These are Table 9.5. With ten years the standard of 100% is the worst year, and
TVaR reaches 100 from 90% up, which is why the monograph's main example speaks
of full capitalization: assets of 100, the largest loss. With only ten
scenarios a 99.5% standard would also be the worst year, so the example uses
the cleanest one.

## 3. Calibrating five distortions

The monograph prices by a **distortion** (a spectral risk measure): a function
`g` that raises the probability of bad outcomes before taking the expected
loss. A distortion is chosen from a family and then calibrated, here to one
requirement: the whole book earns a 15% return on capital, with assets of 100.
The expected loss is 46.6, so the premium `P` and capital `Q = 100 - P` must
satisfy `P - 46.6 = 0.15 Q`, which gives `P = 53.565`. Each of five families, a
constant cost of capital (CCoC), proportional hazard (PH), Wang, dual power and
TVaR, has one parameter, and `calibrate_portfolio()` finds the value that hits
that premium:

```{r}
FAMILIES <- c("ccoc", "ph", "wang", "dual", "tvar")
distortions <- lapply(stats::setNames(FAMILIES, FAMILIES), function(family) {
  calibrate_portfolio(insco, family, assets = 100, return_on_capital = 0.15)
})
for (family in FAMILIES) {
  value <- distortions[[family]]@parameters
  cat(sprintf("%-5s %-7s %.3f\n", family, names(value), value))
}
```

```text
ccoc  r       0.150
ph    rho     0.720
wang  lambda  0.343
dual  beta    1.595
tvar  p       0.271
```

Table 9.3 prints 0.150, 0.720, 0.343, 1.595 and 0.271 for these parameters, and
the values agree. Mind the names: in `aggregate` the CCoC distortion is built
from a risk discount `d = 0.15 / 1.15`, in prospicio from the cost of capital
`r = 0.15`, and `distortion("ccoc", 0.15)` is the same function.

## 4. The price and its allocation to units

With a distortion calibrated, `natural_price()` returns the premium of the
loss capped at the assets, and the **natural allocation** of it to the units,
as a data frame with one row per unit and a `"total"` row: each unit pays the
distorted average of its own loss in the bad years, so a unit that loses most
when the total is large pays more. With `allocation = "linear"` the assets are
also split by expected shares above the asset level.

```{r}
BOOK_LINEAR <- c(A = 13.739, B = 18.522, C = 21.304) # Table 9.6 for CCoC: premium by unit
priced <- natural_price(insco, distortions$ccoc, assets = 100, allocation = "linear")
cat(sprintf("%-6s %7s %7s %7s %7s %7s %6s\n", "", "L", "a", "Q", "P", "M", "COC"))
for (i in seq_len(nrow(priced))) {
  u <- priced[i, ]
  name <- if (u$unit == "total") "Total" else u$unit
  margin <- u$premium - u$loss
  cat(sprintf("%-6s %7.3f %7.3f %7.3f %7.3f %7.3f %6.3f\n", name, u$loss, u$assets,
              u$capital, u$premium, margin, margin / u$capital))
}
```

```text
             L       a       Q       P       M    COC
A       13.400  16.000   2.261  13.739   0.339  0.150
B       18.300  20.000   1.478  18.522   0.222  0.150
C       14.900  64.000  42.696  21.304   6.404  0.150
Total   46.600 100.000  46.435  53.565   6.965  0.150
```

This is Table 9.6, the "industry standard" CCoC pricing: every unit earns 15%
on the capital allocated to it, because that is what the capital was allocated
to mean. Unit C takes 64 of the 100 of assets and pays 21.3 of the premium for
an expected loss of 14.9, so most of the margin (6.4 of 7.0) is C's. The
units' premiums add up to the 53.565 of the book. The data frame also carries
each row's `margin`, `loss_ratio` and `return_on_capital`; the chunk computes
the margin and its return by hand to show where they come from.

The same premium holds for every distortion in the five, because each was
calibrated to it; the distortions differ in who pays. The monograph's Table 9.8
shows the premiums by unit, and they agree here:

```{r}
BOOK_P <- list( # Table 9.8, premium by unit (A, B, C)
  ccoc = c(13.739, 18.522, 21.304),
  ph = c(14.060, 18.349, 21.156),
  wang = c(14.109, 18.637, 20.819),
  dual = c(14.127, 19.117, 20.322),
  tvar = c(13.783, 20.412, 19.371)
)
units_only <- function(priced) priced[priced$unit != "total", ]
cat(sprintf("%-5s %20s %20s %20s\n", "", "A", "B", "C"))
for (family in FAMILIES) {
  got <- units_only(natural_price(insco, distortions[[family]], assets = 100))$premium
  cells <- sprintf("%7.3f (book %6.3f)", got, BOOK_P[[family]])
  cat(sprintf("%-5s ", family), paste(cells, collapse = " "), "\n", sep = "")
}
```

```text
                         A                    B                    C
ccoc   13.739 (book 13.739)  18.522 (book 18.522)  21.304 (book 21.304)
ph     14.060 (book 14.060)  18.349 (book 18.349)  21.156 (book 21.156)
wang   14.109 (book 14.109)  18.637 (book 18.637)  20.819 (book 20.819)
dual   14.127 (book 14.127)  19.117 (book 19.117)  20.322 (book 20.322)
tvar   13.783 (book 13.783)  20.412 (book 20.412)  19.371 (book 19.371)
```

All fifteen premiums match to the three decimals printed. The pattern across
the rows is the substance: the CCoC prices unit C at 21.3 and unit B at 18.5,
the TVaR prices B at 20.4 and C at 19.4. TVaR charges for the units' losses in
the worst years only, where B's 20 is a larger share of the total than its
average share; CCoC charges for the volume of capital each unit consumes, and C
uses 64 of the 100. Neither is the right answer; the distortion is a statement
about what you are paid to bear (see
[Risk loads and distortions](risk-loads-and-distortions.md)).

## 5. Capital by unit, if you must

The monograph's section 8.3 advises against allocating capital, because layers
of capital cost different amounts, and allocates margin instead. If you must
say how much capital each unit uses, it describes a method that allocates each
layer of the asset range by the units' shares of that layer's margin, and sums
over layers. In prospicio this is `allocation = "lifted"`:

```{r}
BOOK_Q <- list( # Table 9.8, capital by unit (A, B, C)
  ccoc = c(4.874, 5.288, 36.273),
  ph = c(7.074, 6.565, 32.796),
  wang = c(8.411, 8.691, 29.333),
  dual = c(8.873, 9.143, 28.419),
  tvar = c(9.034, 9.247, 28.154)
)
cat(sprintf("%-5s %20s %20s %20s\n", "", "A", "B", "C"))
for (family in FAMILIES) {
  lifted <- natural_price(insco, distortions[[family]], assets = 100, allocation = "lifted")
  cells <- sprintf("%7.3f (book %6.3f)", units_only(lifted)$capital, BOOK_Q[[family]])
  cat(sprintf("%-5s ", family), paste(cells, collapse = " "), "\n", sep = "")
}
```

```text
                         A                    B                    C
ccoc    2.261 (book  4.874)   1.478 (book  5.288)  42.696 (book 36.273)
ph      6.481 (book  7.074)   5.597 (book  6.565)  34.356 (book 32.796)
wang    8.411 (book  8.411)   8.691 (book  8.691)  29.333 (book 29.333)
dual    8.873 (book  8.873)   9.143 (book  9.143)  28.419 (book 28.419)
tvar    9.034 (book  9.034)   9.247 (book  9.247)  28.154 (book 28.154)
```

Wang, dual power and TVaR agree with the monograph to three decimals. **CCoC
and PH do not.** The monograph prints a CCoC capital of 4.874, 5.288 and
36.273, and `aggregate` 0.30.1 returns exactly those; prospicio returns 2.261,
1.478 and 42.696, the same as the linear allocation, and a PH capital that is
6.481, 5.597 and 34.356 against the printed 7.074, 6.565 and 32.796. Premiums
and margins are identical in both programs; only the split of capital between
units differs.

The difference is between versions of `aggregate`, not between prospicio and
`aggregate`. The monograph's code ran on `aggregate` 0.24.0, and 0.30.1 prints
the monograph's numbers. prospicio's natural allocation is tested in CI
against reference values computed with `aggregate` 1.0.1 on this very company,
at 1e-10, for both allocations and all five distortions, and those reference
values for CCoC and PH are prospicio's: 2.261, 1.478 and 42.696 for CCoC. So
the lifted capital for these two families changed between 0.30.1 and 1.0.1.
The CCoC value is also what the monograph's own argument implies: under a CCoC
every layer of capital earns the same 15%, so a unit's capital is its margin
divided by 0.15, and unit A's margin of 0.339 gives 2.261. Use the premiums
and margins, which agree everywhere, and treat capital by unit under CCoC and
PH as version dependent; the monograph advises against allocating capital for
much the same reason.

## 6. The reinsurance decision

Chapter 5 asks what a reinsurance cover does to the price of the book. The
monograph's example is an aggregate stop loss of 35 excess of 65: the reinsurer
pays whatever the year's total exceeds 65, up to 35. On these ten years it pays
in one year only, the 100, which is 35 with probability 0.1, a mean of 3.5.
Treating the cover's recovery and the net loss as two units of a new portfolio
prices the cover, and shows what the retained book then needs:

```{r}
stop_loss <- function(total, attach = 65, limit = 35) pmin(pmax(total - attach, 0), limit)

split <- cbind(Net = totals - stop_loss(totals), Ceded = stop_loss(totals))
reinsured <- capital_portfolio(split)
cat("means", reinsured@expected, " (book: net 43.1, ceded 3.5)\n")

BOOK_RE <- list( # Table 9.10, premium and margin of ceded and net, (ceded, net)
  ccoc = c(7.609, 4.109, 45.957, 2.857),
  ph = c(6.662, 3.162, 46.903, 3.803),
  wang = c(6.087, 2.587, 47.478, 4.378),
  dual = c(5.415, 1.915, 48.151, 5.051),
  tvar = c(4.803, 1.303, 48.762, 5.662)
)
cat(sprintf("%-5s %8s %7s %8s %7s\n", "", "ceded P", "M", "net P", "M"))
for (family in FAMILIES) {
  r <- natural_price(reinsured, distortions[[family]], assets = 100)
  ceded <- r[r$unit == "Ceded", ]
  net <- r[r$unit == "Net", ]
  cat(sprintf("%-5s %8.3f %7.3f %8.3f %7.3f   book %s\n", family,
              ceded$premium, ceded$premium - ceded$loss, net$premium, net$premium - net$loss,
              paste(sprintf("%.3f", BOOK_RE[[family]]), collapse = " ")))
}
```

```text
means 43.1 3.5  (book: net 43.1, ceded 3.5)
       ceded P       M    net P       M
ccoc     7.609   4.109   45.957   2.857   book 7.609 4.109 45.957 2.857
ph       6.662   3.162   46.903   3.803   book 6.662 3.162 46.903 3.803
wang     6.087   2.587   47.478   4.378   book 6.087 2.587 47.478 4.378
dual     5.415   1.915   48.151   5.051   book 5.415 1.915 48.151 5.051
tvar     4.803   1.303   48.762   5.662   book 4.803 1.303 48.762 5.662
```

The reinsurer's price depends strongly on the distortion. The cover protects
only against the one worst year, so the risk loads are in the tail: a CCoC
prices it at 7.609 (a margin of 4.109, more than the expected loss of 3.5), and
a dual power at 5.415. Which one is the right yardstick for the reinsurer's
price, or for the buyer's willingness to pay, is the question of the
monograph's chapter 6. The method's contribution is that the answer is on one
page for every yardstick. The two margins always add up to the book's 6.965,
so a dearer cover (CCoC) leaves the retained book less margin (2.857) than a
cheaper one (the dual power leaves 5.051).

## 7. A more realistic example

The last section of the monograph's chapter 9 builds a book from frequency and
severity: three units, Auto, GL and WC, with lognormal severities limited per
claim and a mixed-Poisson (gamma-mixed) count each, compounded by FFT, then
tied together by Iman-Conover rank correlation and priced at a 99.5% standard
and a 15% return. In R a unit is `discretize()` by the local moment method,
`map_grid()` for the per-claim limit, `mixed_poisson_count()` and
`compound_distribution(..., method = "fft")`, whose grid keeps the FFT's
checks in its `report`:

```{r}
compound_unit <- function(loss, limit, mean, cv, mixing_cv, step, points) {
  # A unit: expected loss, a per-claim limit, a lognormal, a gamma mixed count.
  severity <- discretize(lognormal_from_mean_cv(mean, cv), step, points, "local_moment")
  claim <- map_grid(severity, function(x) pmin(x, limit))$grid
  claims <- loss / mean(claim)
  annual <- compound_distribution(mixed_poisson_count(claims, mixing_cv), claim, points,
                                  method = "fft")
  list(claims = claims, claim_mean = mean(claim), annual = annual, report = annual@report)
}

UNITS <- list(
  Auto = list(5000, 5000, 50, 2.0, 0.2, 0.25, 2^16),
  GL = list(3000, 2500, 75, 3.0, 0.3, 0.25, 2^16),
  WC = list(7000, 25000, 5, 10.0, 0.25, 0.25, 2^17)
)
annual <- list()
cat(sprintf("%-5s %8s %11s %9s %7s %10s\n", "", "claims", "claim mean", "agg mean",
            "agg cv", "tail mass"))
for (name in names(UNITS)) {
  unit <- do.call(compound_unit, UNITS[[name]])
  a <- annual[[name]] <- unit$annual
  cat(sprintf("%-5s %8.1f %11.3f %9.1f %7.3f %10.1e\n", name, unit$claims, unit$claim_mean,
              mean(a), sqrt(variance(a)) / mean(a), unit$report$tail_mass))
}
```

```text
        claims  claim mean  agg mean  agg cv  tail mass
Auto     100.0      49.982    5000.0   0.298    2.3e-06
GL        41.0      73.156    3000.0   0.502    4.4e-07
WC      1401.1       4.996    6999.7   0.349    1.6e-04
```

The monograph prints (Table 9.11) 100.0, 41.008 and 1,401.1 claims, mean
claims of 49.982, 73.156 and 4.996 (4.945 as achieved on its grid), and
aggregate CVs of 0.298, 0.502 and 0.349. The numbers agree. Unit WC drives the
tail, with a thick severity and a high limit.

Iman-Conover pairs the units' draws so that their rank correlations match a
target without changing any unit's distribution. Draw each unit at evenly
spaced quantiles, tie them with the monograph's matrix (Table 9.12) by
`iman_conover()` on a `predictive_distribution()` with one component per
unit, and build a portfolio from the result with `capital_portfolio()`, which
reads each simulation as an equally likely scenario (Python's
`Portfolio.from_predictive`):

```{r}
TARGET <- rbind(c(1.0, 0.5, 0.4), c(0.5, 1.0, 0.1), c(0.4, 0.1, 1.0))

correlated_portfolio <- function(n_sims, seed) {
  q <- (seq_len(n_sims) - 0.5) / n_sims
  draws <- sapply(annual, function(g) quantile(g, q)) # n_sims rows, one column per unit
  keys <- data.frame(unit = names(annual))
  joint <- iman_conover(predictive_distribution(draws, keys), TARGET, seed)
  capital_portfolio(joint)
}

book <- correlated_portfolio(50000, 4817)
cat("units", book@units, " means", sprintf("%.1f", book@expected), "\n")
```

```text
units Auto GL WC  means 5000.0 3000.0 6999.7
```

Now calibrate the five distortions to a 15% return at the 99.5% standard
(Table 9.16) and price each unit (Table 9.17):

```{r}
BOOK_PARAMS <- c(ccoc = 0.150, ph = 0.654, wang = 0.437, dual = 1.756, tvar = 0.299)
priced_book <- list()
cat(sprintf("assets at 99.5%%: %s   (book 28,898)\n", comma(portfolio_assets(book, 0.995))))
for (family in FAMILIES) {
  d <- calibrate_portfolio(book, family, p = 0.995, return_on_capital = 0.15)
  pb <- priced_book[[family]] <- natural_price(book, d, p = 0.995)
  cells <- paste(sprintf("%8.1f", units_only(pb)$premium), collapse = " ")
  cat(sprintf("%-5s parameter %.3f (book %.3f)   premium Auto, GL, WC: %s   total %s\n",
              family, d@parameters, BOOK_PARAMS[[family]], cells,
              comma(pb$premium[pb$unit == "total"], 1)))
}
```

```text
assets at 99.5%: 28,448   (book 28,898)
ccoc  parameter 0.150 (book 0.150)   premium Auto, GL, WC:   5351.0   3230.1   8154.6   total 16,735.8
ph    parameter 0.654 (book 0.654)   premium Auto, GL, WC:   5483.4   3377.8   7874.6   total 16,735.8
wang  parameter 0.434 (book 0.437)   premium Auto, GL, WC:   5511.0   3405.1   7819.6   total 16,735.8
dual  parameter 1.740 (book 1.756)   premium Auto, GL, WC:   5529.0   3421.1   7785.6   total 16,735.8
tvar  parameter 0.291 (book 0.299)   premium Auto, GL, WC:   5536.0   3423.9   7776.0   total 16,735.8
```

The parameters are within about 0.01 of Table 9.16 (the PH parameter is equal;
the TVaR level is 0.291 against 0.299), and the total premium of about 16,740
is close to the monograph's 16,800.3. They are not expected to agree exactly.
The monograph's sample has 1,000 simulations, so its 99.5% quantile rests on
five points, while the draws here are 50,000 and evenly spaced. How much a
sample of 1,000 moves the answer is easy to see by running the same
calculation on samples of different sizes:

```{r}
for (run in list(c(1000, 11), c(1000, 12), c(10000, 11), c(50000, 11))) {
  pf <- correlated_portfolio(run[1], run[2])
  d <- calibrate_portfolio(pf, "ccoc", p = 0.995, return_on_capital = 0.15)
  p <- natural_price(pf, d, p = 0.995)
  tot <- p[p$unit == "total", ]
  cat(sprintf("%6d sims, seed %d: assets %9s  premium %9s\n", run[1], run[2],
              comma(tot$assets), comma(tot$premium, 1)))
}
```

```text
  1000 sims, seed 11: assets    27,850  premium  16,657.6
  1000 sims, seed 12: assets    29,368  premium  16,855.1
 10000 sims, seed 11: assets    28,692  premium  16,771.1
 50000 sims, seed 11: assets    28,520  premium  16,744.9
```

The premium moves by a percent or two between two samples of 1,000 and settles
as the sample grows, so numbers from a small sample are not worth quoting to
four digits. For more units, more events and a real model, the monograph's
advice is the same: more simulations, and a capital standard you can defend.

The seeded samples are the same in R and Python: `iman_conover()` runs the
same Rust code from the same seed, so these four lines and the table above
equal the Python guide's. One number needs care: the second sample's assets
are 29,368.5 exactly, and the `comma()` helper of the setup chunk rounds that
half to even, as Python does. R's `sprintf("%.0f", 29368.5)` prints 29369 on
Windows and 29368 on Linux.

## 8. What this guide leaves out

- **Chapters 1 and 2** (the charter of a capital model, business operations,
  reinsurance, asset risk, the economic scenario generator, accounting): the
  organisation around the model, with no calculation to reproduce.
- **Chapter 5's** new business pricing, mergers and acquisitions and portfolio
  optimization, and **chapter 6's** selection of a distortion from a range.
  The distortions and the natural allocation they need are here; the decisions
  built on them are the monograph's to explain.
- **Section 8.4**, Bodoff's layer capital allocation, is available as
  `bodoff_allocation()`; the monograph gives it as a comparison and no figures
  to check against.
- **Capital by unit under CCoC and PH** (section 5): version dependent, see the
  note there.

Where to go next (these guides are written in Python, and the R functions
named above do the same work):
[Risk loads and distortions](risk-loads-and-distortions.md) for which
distortion to use and how to calibrate it to a quote,
[Aggregate distributions](aggregate-distributions.md) for the compound
distributions of section 7, and
[prospicio for aggregate users](prospicio-for-aggregate-users.md) for the
package behind the monograph's code.
